extracted.intended_audience: crisis managers, public relations practitioners, organizational communicators, and students/researchers of crisis communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing crisis situations (type, history, prior reputation) and selecting evidence-based communication responses to protect organizational reputation following Coombs' Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial crisis responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: How much the organization's stakeholders attribute the crisis to the organization; how responsible key publics hold the organization for the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing initial crisis responsibility is the first step in evaluating reputational threat and selecting an appropriate response strategy; greater perceived responsibility increases reputational threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational threat
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of damage a crisis could inflict on an organization if no action is taken to respond to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputational threat is influenced by three elements: (1) initial crisis responsibility, (2) crisis history, and (3) prior relational reputation. Use predicted reputational threat to choose response strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis history
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the organization has faced similar crises in the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence of a crisis history intensifies attributions of organization responsibility and increases reputational threat; presence of history pushes responses toward more accommodative strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior relational reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: How well an organization has treated its stakeholders in the past—the organization's pre-crisis relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative prior relational reputation increases attributions of responsibility and reputational threat; positive or neutral prior reputation can reduce perceived responsibility and temper response choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis cluster typology (victim / accidental / intentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT differentiates crises into three clusters: victim (organization is also a victim; weak attributions of responsibility), accidental (organizational actions were unintentional; minimal attributions), and intentional/preventable (organization knowingly placed people at risk; strong attributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which cluster a crisis falls into to predict stakeholder attributions and the likely severity of reputational threat; use cluster + history + prior reputation to select strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table 1 guideline 1: Informing/adjusting for low-attribution victim crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Informing and adjusting information alone can be enough when crises have minimal attributions of crisis responsibility (victim crises), no history of similar crises and a neutral or positive prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criteria are met, simple information-focused responses (provide facts, correct misinformation) may suffice; avoid unnecessarily escalatory tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table 1 guideline 2: Use victimage in specific victim cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Victimage can be used as part of the response for workplace violence, product tampering, natural disasters and rumors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remind stakeholders that the organization is also a victim when appropriate to elicit sympathy; ensure the claim is credible and accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table 1 guideline 3: Diminish for victim crises with history or poor reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish crisis response strategies should be used for crises with minimal attributions of crisis responsibility (victim crises) coupled with a history of similar crises and/or negative prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If history or poor prior reputation increases threat, move from pure informational responses toward diminish tactics that lessen perceived responsibility, supported by credible evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table 1 guideline 4: Diminish for low-attribution accident crises with no history/positive rep
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish crisis response strategies should be used for crises with low attributions of crisis responsibility (accident crises), which have no history of similar crises, and a neutral or positive prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For accidental crises without negative history, use excuses/justifications to minimize perceived responsibility while providing evidence to support the frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table 1 guideline 5: Rebuild for accident crises with history or negative rep
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild crisis response strategies should be used for crises with low attributions of crisis responsibility (accident crises), coupled with a history of similar crises and/or negative prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accidents occur on a background of history/poor reputation, adopt rebuild strategies (compensation/apology) to repair perceptions and reduce threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table 1 guideline 6: Rebuild for strong-attribution/preventable crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild crisis response strategies should be used for crises with strong attributions of crisis responsibility (preventable crises) regardless of crisis history or prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If stakeholders strongly attribute fault to the organization (preventable/intentional cluster), prioritize rebuild strategies (apology, compensation, corrective action) to mitigate reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table 1 guideline 7: Deny for rumor and challenge crises when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The deny posture crisis response strategies should be used for rumor and challenge crises, when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a crisis is a rumor or challenge and can be credibly disproved, use denial/attack-accuser/scapegoating tactics to sever perceived connection between organization and crisis; ensure evidence supports denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table 1 guideline 8: Maintain consistency in crisis response strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistency in crisis response strategies. Mixing deny crisis response strategies with either the diminish or rebuild strategies will erode the effectiveness of the overall response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contradictory messages (e.g., denying while also apologizing); inconsistent mixes reduce credibility and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary strategy: Deny
rubrics_metrics.description: Deny strategies attempt to establish a crisis frame that severs any perceived connection between the organization and the crisis (e.g., assert no crisis, attack accuser, scapegoat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deny only when the organization is not involved or when the crisis can be credibly dispelled; inappropriate denials risk further reputational harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deny tactic: Attack the accuser
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis manager confronts the person or group claiming something is wrong with the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confrontation can be used to challenge false claims but may escalate conflict; use cautiously and ensure factual basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deny tactic: Denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis manager asserts that there is no crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only effective when credible evidence removes doubt; false or weak denials can backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deny tactic: Scapegoat
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis manager blames some person or group outside of the organization for the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting blame may protect reputation if accurate and defensible, but can erode trust if perceived as shirking responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary strategy: Diminish
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish responses attempt to assure publics that the crisis is not as bad as it seems or that the organization had nothing to do with the situation; they lessen the connection between the organization and the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diminish strategies require credible evidence; if conflicting frames appear in media, publics adopt the most credible source's frame. Use excuses or justifications supported by facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminish tactic: Excuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis manager minimizes organizational responsibility by denying intent to do harm and/or claiming inability to control the events that triggered the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excuses can reduce perceived culpability but must be plausible and supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminish tactic: Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis manager minimizes the perceived damage caused by the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the outcomes as less severe or explain mitigating circumstances; use verifiable data where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary strategy: Rebuild
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild strategies attempt to change perceptions by offering real or symbolic aid to victims and asking forgiveness; they are used when attributions of responsibility are stronger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuild is appropriate when responsibility is high or history/prior reputation demand reparative action; actions must be sincere and substantive to restore trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild tactic: Compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis manager offers money or other gifts to victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary or other tangible compensation can reduce negative perception when feasible; ensure fairness and avoid perceptions of buying silence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild tactic: Apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis manager indicates the organization takes full responsibility for the crisis and asks stakeholders for forgiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sincere apology includes acceptance of responsibility and corrective commitments; hollow or conditional apologies may be ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary strategy: Bolstering
rubrics_metrics.description: Bolstering presents new, positive information about the organization and/or reminds stakeholders of past good works to increase positive reputational perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolstering can arouse sympathy and goodwill but should be used to supplement primary responses (deny/diminish/rebuild), not replace them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolstering tactic: Reminder
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell stakeholders about the past good works of the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to balance negative perceptions but avoid appearing to distract from responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolstering tactic: Ingratiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis manager praises stakeholders and/or reminds them of past good works by the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can soften stakeholder attitudes but should not substitute for corrective action when responsibility exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolstering tactic: Victimage
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis managers remind stakeholders that the organization is a victim of the crisis too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate when the organization legitimately suffered; use carefully to avoid appearing to deflect responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media framing influence
rubrics_metrics.description: How the crisis is framed in the media will determine how the organization's publics view the situation; the media's frames become stakeholders’ frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get your side of the story into the media; inconsistent or non-credible framing risks losing the battle for stakeholder perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological/emotional effects on publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived levels of crisis responsibility influence emotions (e.g., high responsibility → anger; low responsibility → sympathy), which in turn affect behaviors toward the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate emotional reactions when selecting strategies; responses should aim to reduce negative emotions and promote positive behavioral outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of crisis response strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis response strategies have three objectives relative to protecting reputations: (1) shape attributions of the crisis, (2) change perceptions of the organization in crisis, and (3) reduce the negative effect generated by the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and execute strategies that explicitly target these objectives; measure success in terms of changed attributions, perceptions, and behavioral outcomes.
